newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sudan said using "scorched earth" against rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sudan said using "scorched earth" against rebels.

text.p: A Swiss-based Christian organisation said on Friday Sudan had launched a "scorched earth" policy in areas in the east of the country where it was facing a mounting challenge by rebels.

Christian Solidarity International (CSI) said a two-member team it send on a covert visit last week to the south of Sudan's Blue Nile region reported that government forces were "bombing and torching" villages right across the area.

"The government of Sudan is waging a new scorched earth policy against its own civilians in the closed areas of east-central Sudan near the Etiopian border," said a statement from CSI, which has its headquarters in Zurich.
"Since the village-razing programme was launched last Spring, at least 50,000 people have been forced to flee from their homes," the statement declared.

Most of the displaced -- which CSI said included Moslems as well as Christians and animists -- were now living in makeshift shelters or in the open "and are reduced to scavenging for nuts, roots and fruit.

"Many are now dying of starvation and disease," the statement said, citing its team -- British parliamentarian Baroness Caroline Cox and CSI official John Eibner, who have both made previous undercover visits to Sudan.

In a letter to United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata and High Commissioner for Human Rights Jose Ayala Lasso, CSI appealed for action to start urgent emergency airdrops of food and medicines to the displaced.

"The destruction of villages is accomplished by a combination of aerial bombardment with Antonov bombers and helicopter gunships, in conjunction with ground attacks by the government of Sudan's regular army and various government- supported militias," CSI said.
The latest attack, it added, occurred on January 3 when government troops raided and torched the village of Pakeg, some 50 km (30 miles) south of the town of Yabus.

Government policy, CSI declared, appeared intended to punish the local population for supporting the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) -- which earlier on Friday said it had captured the town of Maban in the Blue Nile region.
The area has long been closed to U.N. and other international relief agencies who have been refused permission to go there by the authorities in the capital, Khartoum.
CSI said Eibner and Baroness Cox, a member of the british House of Lords, had delivered one tonne of emergency medical supplies to the refugees.

"But much more is needed to sustain the destitute displaced population in their own land and to avert a major humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Ethiopia" to where several thousand had fled, the statement added.
Failure by the international community to launch an emergency relief operation were mounted immedtiately, CSI said, "will condemn thousands to death by starvation and disease."
